findings.passage: The essay's most unusual commitment was about his own company, a step he said Anthropic was "unilaterally committing to."
findings.problem: The opening cuts the quote short. The essay (S09, opened) says the first step is something Anthropic is "unilaterally committing to (and calls on governments to require other frontier companies to match)." It twice urges other frontier companies to "follow suit." It says the most effective pacing is "regulation that targets all US frontier AI companies." It also keeps Anthropic's right to redact "security-sensitive, legally privileged, commercially sensitive, or third-party confidential information." Axios (S41, opened) reports that Altman agreed the same day and said OpenAI would also give access to external evaluators. The draft then calls this "an odd offer" from a company preparing an IPO. That framing treats the commitment as costly self-binding. Before an IPO, though, verifiable safety also builds credibility, and a standard that governments impose on rivals is exactly what the Palihapitiya and Nvidia regulatory-capture critique describes. The Six thesis ("rules that bind him") and the Type 5 FAQ both lean on this hook.
findings.acceptance_test: The hook, or the paragraph after it, states that the same sentence asks governments to require competitors to match the commitment, and mentions the redaction carve-out. Where the evaluators are used as evidence, the article notes Altman's same-day matching pledge (Axios, September 12, 2026). Either "odd offer" is removed, or the pre-IPO credibility reading follows it. The FAQ "Why isn't Dario Amodei a Type 5?" no longer presents the evaluator invitation as pure self-binding.

findings.passage: What tips this page toward personality is that the reflexes predate the company
findings.problem: The rebuttal tests personality only against Anthropic's commercial interest. Two documented alternatives in opened sources also predate Anthropic. (a) Control-seeking: Big Technology (S01) reports that "Within OpenAI, some saw Amodei's focus on safety as a route to control the company altogether." (b) Learned practice and milieu: according to the WSJ (S13), "Dario and Karnofsky" made the 2016 "tell the government first" argument together in a shared group house. Holden Karnofsky, Daniela's fiancé at the time, founded an effective-altruism philanthropy, and the Journal calls EA one of the first communities to take AI danger seriously. AFP (S14) says Amodei "is considered a leading figure in the effective altruism and rationalism movements." It also quotes an anonymous witness saying his interest in "both AI and Effective Altruism" "determined his trajectory." Anthropic told AFP that he does not identify as part of the EA community. The draft never mentions EA, Karnofsky or the OpenAI-era control reading. A community whose norms already prescribe threat-modeling, coordination regimes and telling the government first explains the same pre-Anthropic reflexes. The standard requires comparing learned practices with the type explanation.
findings.acceptance_test: The non-type paragraph names both the OpenAI-era control reading and the EA/rationalist milieu, with attribution. It includes Anthropic's statement that he does not identify as EA, and notes that the 2016 argument was made jointly with Karnofsky. It then either offers an observation that neither the milieu nor incentives would predict, or downgrades "tips this page" to a stated limit. The medium-confidence type answer remains consistent with whichever it chooses.

findings.passage: His anger in this record targets dishonesty, bad faith and broken promises.
findings.problem: This generalizes from a curated sample. The WSJ piece the draft relies on (S13, opened) records anger with other targets. In 2018 Dario "got angry that he had been left out of the loop" when Brockman and Altman met Barack Obama. He called Brockman's $25 million donation to a pro-Trump super PAC "evil." He compared the Musk-Altman legal fight to the fight between Hitler and Stalin. Anger at being excluded from credit is not anger at a broken promise. It fits the recognition strand the page sets aside in "What the type doesn't settle." Moral condemnation of a rival's politics fits a Type 1 judgment. Two of the four public examples (the "doomer" label and Huang's line) are anger at others misreading his own motives, which a reputation or image reading also predicts. So "It fits a Six, whose alarm is tuned to betrayal" does not beat the alternatives on the full record.
findings.acceptance_test: Either the section includes the left-out-of-the-loop episode, attributed to the Journal's unnamed sources (the Hitler/Stalin wording need not be quoted), and explains how the Six reading handles anger at exclusion, or the claim is narrowed to his public anger with a note that the Journal also reports anger over exclusion and credit. The Type 1 contrast sentence still holds against the "evil" remark, or it is revised.

findings.problem: The draft uses the Journal's facts about conditional loyalty but leaves out the Journal's own reading of the same events. S13 says the reasons for the departure "also include personal wounds that have never healed, including jockeying over more classic corporate issues such as power and credit." It describes the GPT turf fight: Dario, then research director, wanted Brockman "nowhere near" the language project and listed reasons in a staff meeting, including Radford's preference. Radford was "mortified, feeling like his preferences were being used in a proxy war between senior executives." Seen that way, the conditions Amodei set read as turf and status as easily as tested trust: Brockman and Sutskever not in charge, reporting only to the board, and he "couldn't work with Brockman." The anger section has the same problem. It presents the tobacco comparison as private anger, but the Journal's next sentence calls it a "brand strategy" that casts Anthropic as the "healthy alternative." Keeping a source's facts while dropping its interpretation that cuts against the thesis is a context-fidelity failure.
findings.acceptance_test: "Staying on conditions" states the Journal's power-and-credit framing. It gives enough of the Brockman/GPT dispute, attributed to unnamed sources, for the reader to see the turf reading next to the trust reading. The tobacco comparison is either labeled as part of what the Journal calls an internal brand strategy or dropped as evidence of private anger. After these additions, the conditional-loyalty argument either still stands or is explicitly weakened.

findings.passage: He looks for a structure strong enough to hold it, and he doesn't exempt himself.
findings.problem: The ending settles in the subject's favor what the article earlier says it cannot settle. "What the type doesn't settle" lists the board-only reporting demand and the reported super-voting shares, and concedes "From outside, securing a safe base and grabbing control look the same." The final section then rests on his own self-descriptions: discomfort with private control, and being "often turned off" by leaders who sound like prophets. Meanwhile it omits the most direct adverse characterization in the opened record. Under Secretary Emil Michael called him "a liar" with a "God complex" who wants "to personally control the U.S military" (Fortune, February 27, 2026, S18, opened). Big Technology (S01) reports the OpenAI-era view that his safety focus was "a route to control the company altogether." A counterparty's insult is not evidence of motive, but the conclusion should not assert the opposite as established.
findings.acceptance_test: "He doesn't exempt himself" is attributed or qualified (for example, "in what he proposes, he doesn't exempt himself") and points back to the unresolved control evidence. The control charge (Michael's words and/or the OpenAI-era reading) appears once, with attribution and context. The final paragraph does not present his self-description as the answer to that charge.

findings.passage: The lesson of his father's death is that delay has a body count. It explains why he keeps building.
findings.problem: These two author-voice sentences turn his own account into the established cause of his career. The record offers other or additional reasons. The pacing essay quoted in this draft's introduction gives his reason for building as benefits and keeping AI out of the hands of "authoritarian powers." Wired (C08) says he had already found physics "too removed from the real world." AFP's anonymous witness credits AI and EA with having "determined his trajectory." The draft itself shows him using the father story inside arguments: "You heard what I just said, my father died...", the Baker reply, and the essay's "I feel the urgency personally." Of the disclosures, the draft says "Both readings fit." The heading "A cure that came a few years late" adopts his timeline as fact, although the evidence record notes that sofosbuvir was approved about seven years after 2006 (C09, C71). The Jade Wang FAQ line "lost time, not abstract futurism, sits underneath his urgency" claims more than her quote supports.
findings.acceptance_test: The causal sentence is attributed or hedged ("In his telling..." or "This suggests..."), and at least one competing explanation is named. The heading either attributes the gap or drops "a few years." If the Jade Wang FAQ wording is locked by its packet, the body does not repeat that causal claim as settled.

findings.passage: That is the counterphobic Six in one week
findings.problem: This asserts the type in author voice for an event the record also explains as a company position and a brand move. The Pentagon's side is missing. Fortune (S18) reports that the department said it "has no intention of conducting mass surveillance or removing humans from weapons-targeting decisions," and that the dispute "could rest on how each side is defining 'autonomous' or 'surveillance' in practice." It also reports that OpenAI and xAI accepted "all lawful purposes" terms. That made Anthropic's refusal a market differentiator, consistent with the "healthy alternative" strategy the WSJ describes. The commercial alternative appears only three sections later, and only in general terms.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence becomes a hedged reading ("This fits..."). The section itself adds one attributed sentence on the Pentagon's stated position and one on the commercial or brand reading. The Type 1 line stays.

findings.passage: The brake he set in advance
findings.problem: The heading presents the September 2026 change as a pre-committed brake being pulled. The essay (S09) names two concrete triggers instead. First, AI "advancing drastically faster" since "roughly this summer" through recursive self-improvement. Second, the OpenAI-Hugging Face agent incident. It also mentions Anthropic's own "recent alignment incidents." Axios (S41) places the essay in the week of an Anthropic employee's "very public resignation" and "a sudden surge of public and congressional outrage." On CBS he said he hadn't "fully just appreciated" how fast progress would feel, which is the opposite of a pre-set rule working as planned. Axios also notes that Anthropic "has gone back and forth." The draft names neither stated trigger, so a change made in reaction to events reads as a pre-commitment carried out, which conveniently supports the Six thesis.
findings.acceptance_test: The heading no longer implies that the 2026 change carried out the July 2025 condition, unless the text shows that condition was met. The section names his two stated triggers and the dated public-pressure context, with attribution.

protected_passages.passage: Read as a Five, he spent a reserved fact when the argument needed it. Read as a Six, he offered proof of sincerity to a public he had just described as in a crisis of trust, with his word attached. Both readings fit, so this page does not lean on them.
protected_passages.reason: An exemplary refusal to count non-discriminating evidence. The draft should apply this same discipline to the anger, father and Pentagon passages.

protected_passages.passage: From outside, securing a safe base and grabbing control look the same.
protected_passages.reason: An honest concession of the strongest adverse reading. Keep it, and let the ending honor it (see critic-05).

protected_passages.passage: The most serious alternative may not be a type at all.
protected_passages.reason: It puts the incentive explanation at type level instead of treating it as a footnote. Strengthen what follows rather than cut it.

protected_passages.passage: Read as a Five, that is independence: go build your own system. The words that matter are in the middle. He takes people he trusts, and the suspicion he names is dishonesty.
protected_passages.reason: A close reading of a primary quote that does real discriminating work and gives the rival reading first.

protected_passages.passage: A lab colleague, Olivier Marre, gave AFP a cooler picture in 2026
protected_passages.reason: Named, adverse, early-life testimony placed right next to admiring testimony. Keep it.

assessment: This draft is more candid than most. It has an "unsettled" section, a type-level incentive alternative, named adverse testimony (Marre, Baker, Palihapitiya) and an honest non-discriminator paragraph. But the adverse evidence sits in those dedicated sections, while the narrative sections tell attractive stories in author voice: the self-binding hook, the father-as-cause line, betrayal-tuned anger, the counterphobic Pentagon week, the pre-set brake and the ending's "doesn't exempt himself." I reopened S09 (pacing essay), S13 (WSJ via To Vima), S01 (Big Technology), S14 (AFP via reader proxy), S18 (Fortune) and S41 (Axios via reader proxy). Each of them contains context that cuts against the story it is cited for. That context is the competitor-binding clause and redaction carve-out in the commitment, Altman's same-day match, the Journal's "power and credit" and "brand strategy" framing, the left-out-of-the-loop anger, the OpenAI-era control reading, the EA/rationalist milieu, the Pentagon's stated position and Michael's "God complex" charge. None of this is a fabrication or a misquote. The quoted words match the sources. The problems are selection and framing. The Six-over-Five case still has real support (conditional loyalty, "people you trust", the evaluators, the G7 request), but it should survive the milieu and control alternatives in the text before "medium confidence" is earned. Similarity: the top trip ("a reading of public evidence") is a shared disclaimer sentence with Arthur Mensch, which is boilerplate and not reportable. The 5-versus-6 tiebreak (Five withdraws, Six builds trusted structure) mirrors the Mensch page's structure, but the evidence here is specific to Amodei, so I filed no reuse finding. Cross-page note for the editor: the Arthur Mensch draft says Amodei reads "as a Five on 9takes", which becomes false if this retype ships. I keep all research risk flags, and the six-role jury is warranted.
